newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-MANY EXPERTS FAVOR HOLYFIELD OVER TYSON.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-MANY EXPERTS FAVOR HOLYFIELD OVER TYSON.

text.p: Two days before Saturday's World Boxing Association's heavyweight title bout, many experts favoured Evander Holyfield to again defeat Mike Tyson even though oddsmakers had it 2-1 the other way.

Holyfield, who took the title away from Tyson by stopping him in the 11th round last November, is even stronger and quicker than in their first bout, training camp members say. And then there is the mental edge that comes from knowing you have already taken your opponent's best shot and beaten him.
Eddie Futch, who trained six heavyweight champions including Joe Frazier, Larry Holmes and Riddick Bowe, is among those seeing Holyfield riding the momentum of the first fight.
"It benefits Holyfield," he said. "Psychologically, Holyfield is going to be higher because he knows he can do it."
"Now Holyfield has so much confidence, it has put him on a different level," said former U.S. Olympic coach Ken Adams. "He has reached heights maybe even Holyfield didn't think he could reach."

"Ring" magazine's Steve Farhood agreed the advantage was with the champion. "That's a huge psychological advantage, especially because Tyson hasn't had an interim fight. To me that's Holyfield's biggest edge."
Muhammad Ali's legendary trainer-manager Angelo Dundee was even quoted as predicting Holyfield would knock out Tyson.

"He's going to get knocked out again," Dundee told USA Today. "In a fighter's life, there's always a guy that can kick his butt. Once you bust that cloak of invincibility, then you got the guy licked."
However, some insiders pointed to the fact that despite losing only three times in 36 fights, Holyfield has not won consecutive title bouts since 1992 and is only 5-3 in his last eight fights.
"I don't think Holyfield will be as good. It's hard for me to believe that he could be that good in back-to-back fights," said one trainer, Miguel Diaz.
Holyfield's sparring partner Gary Bell thinks the 34-year-old champion is even better now than he was 7-1/2 months ago.
"He's much stronger and much sharper this time," he told reporters at the MGM Grand where Holyfield went through a training session Thursday in front of the cameras.
"His combinations are better. He's very serious because he wants to prove to the world that it wasn't a fluke the first time," said Bell.
And he discounted the criticism that Holyfield lacks the big punch of Tyson. "The man can punch hard. Trust me, when he hits you, you feel it," the sparring partner said.

Holyfield's trainer Don Turner said a postponement of the rematch after Tyson cut his eye had not damaged his fighter's training. The trainer, like the sparring partner, said Holyfield was in even better physical shape now than on November 9.
"He is stronger this time because he spent the same amount of time with (conditioning coach Tim) Hallmark. We kept up the strength, we maintained what we had."
Turner said the extra training after the scheduled May 3 fight was postponed had helped Holyfield work even harder.
"Of course, he was disappointed but the delay works to our favour because we worked on a few more things. We got a chance to do a few more drills.
"From what I've been seeing from him, he's better than he was before. He's quicker, he's stronger and he's punching harder," Turner told reporters.
As for Tyson, who turns 31 on Monday, it was difficult to get an assessment of his form because he closed his training camp to the media for the week before the fight.
But according to trainer Richie Giachetti -- who did not train Tyson for the last bout -- his man has to get back to basics for Saturday.
"We're going back to some of the things he learned with the great Cus D'Amato," Giachetti told reporters. "I am bringing Mike back to what he had when he had the title."
What he had then, when he became the youngest heavyweight champion in history at the age of 20, was an intimidating bulldozer style with a killer left hook and knockout right.

"You're going to see the real Mike Tyson, the one who won the title ten years ago," said Giachetti, without elaborating on what Tyson must do differently to avoid the embarrassment of a second loss to the three-time world champion.
